In the beginning, the world was shrouded in endless twilight. The Sun goddess Solara ruled the day with blazing authority, while her brother Noctus commanded the night in absolute darkness. Neither would yield to the other, and so the world knew only harsh extremes.

A young weaver named Lyra grew tired of this division. She could not work in the blinding day or the impenetrable night. So she climbed the highest mountain, carrying her loom, and called out to both deities.

"Great Solara, mighty Noctus," she pleaded, "grant us something between your powers—a gentle light for the darkness, a soft glow that does not burn."

The siblings, moved by her courage, agreed to compromise. Solara plucked a single thread from her golden hair, and Noctus wove it with the silk of shadow. Together, they gave the shimmering strand to Lyra.

She placed it upon her loom and wove throughout the night. By dawn, she had created thousands of tiny lights, each one a perfect balance of day and night. She cast them into the sky, where they scattered across the darkness.

These became the stars—proof that even the mightiest powers can find harmony, and that mortals can inspire the divine.
